title: Mixture of Experts
oneLine: Route each token to a few experts: parameters grow, compute per token does not - and all of them still have to be resident.

paras: A dense layer uses every parameter for every token. An MoE layer holds many expert FFNs and a router that sends each token to the top-k of them, so total parameters can grow enormously while the FLOPs per token stay roughly fixed. That is why MoE models train so well for their compute budget.

The trap is assuming that serving inherits the same win. It does not: every expert must be RESIDENT in memory because any token might route to it, so memory scales with total parameters while compute scales with active ones. A model that trains like a small one serves like a large one.
The layer is a sparse gated combination over experts:
sections.texNote: With k=2 of 64 experts, active parameters are ~1/32 of total - and resident memory is still all of it.

sections.code:
gate = self.router(x)                            # [tokens, n_experts]
w, idx = gate.softmax(-1).topk(self.k, dim=-1)

y = torch.zeros_like(x)
for e in range(self.n_experts):
    sel = (idx == e).any(-1)
    if sel.any():
        y[sel] += w[sel][idx[sel] == e].unsqueeze(-1) * self.experts[e](x[sel])

# without a balance term the router collapses onto a few experts
aux = self.n_experts * (frac_tokens * mean_prob).sum()
sections.caption: The auxiliary load-balancing loss is not optional - left off, routing collapses and most experts go unused.

takeaways: Parameters scale, compute per token does not - that is the training argument.
All experts stay resident, so memory scales with TOTAL parameters and residency bounds the batch.
Routing needs an explicit balance loss or it collapses onto a handful of experts.
